10.27.2.en: The fear of the Lord precedes the pursuit of authority, but in violence and pride is its loss [21].

10.27.3.en: The rich and the dignified (eminent) and the poor are on an equal footing; their boast is the fear of the Lord [22].

10.27.4.en: The greatness and dignity of a man are not in his possessions, nor in his position or abilities, but in his fear of the Lord, his piety and his wisdom, however great his poverty.

10.28.0.en: v Poverty is not a permanent source of pride, but rather voluntary poverty for the sake of the Gospel. This is perfection! Many have been deprived of wealth, yet in their depths they desire it. They were not saved because they are poor, and their inner intention condemns them. He is not happy who lacks everything, but he who considers the commandment better than the treasures of the world. Thus the Lord blesses him: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Mt 5:3). Not those who lack wealth, but those who chose poverty from within their souls. Happiness comes only to him who chose it. For every virtue, especially the virtue of poverty, is a voluntary act [32].

10.28.1.en: St. Basil the Great It is not just that the wise poor man should be dishonored, nor is it fitting that the sinful man should be honored [23].

10.28.2.en: The noble and the judge and the ruler will be honored, and none of them is greater than he who fears the Lord [24].

10.28.3.en: The free render service to a wise servant, and the man of understanding does not murmur at it [25].

10.28.4.en: The wise Solomon says: "A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren" (Prov 17:2). And the Apostle Paul says: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). And also: "Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all" (Col 3:11).

10.28.5.en: v "He that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman" (1 Cor 7:22). The person who is delivered from the sins, which in truth refer to "slaves," becomes the Lord's freeman. For he who walks without wisdom is a slave...

10.29.0.en: This is also the opinion of the ancients, who used to call the wise free, and all who are not wise slaves. It is said: "The free serve a wise slave" (see Sir 10:25). Therefore he who believes, though a slave for a time, becomes the Lord's freeman, because by his faith in Christ he walks in wisdom. Sins create slaves, like Ham the son of Noah, who became a slave because of his sin and his lack of discretion (Gen 9:22-24). And when one receives forgiveness of sins he becomes free [33].

10.30.0.en: 29 Do not excuse yourself from engaging in work, and do not be puffed up in the time of want. 30 For he who busies himself with every work is better than one who goes about or is puffed up while he is in want of bread.

10.30.1.en: Do not show off your wisdom when doing your work, and do not exalt yourself in the time of your distress [26].

10.31.0.en: v Those who spend their lives in small and humble efforts become free from dangers, and have no need of special precautions, and find the way that leads to God with ease, through their constant victory over the passions [34].

10.31.1.en: St. Anthony the Great He who works while possessing much is better than he who boasts but is in need of bread [27].

10.31.2.en: However great a man's wealth, he is in need of work. According to St. Basil the Great, work is necessary for the following reasons: 1. Work is a divine commandment and a divine gift, for God created man to work (Gen 2:15). Without work man loses the taste of life. St. Basil affirms that there is no excuse for the lazy man who lives in idleness while he is able to work. It is fitting for him to imitate those fishes that cross the seas in a wondrous way in search of food [35]. 2. Work helps us to do good, so that we share our resources with those who lack them. It is fitting for the believer to work not only in order to eat, but also for his spiritual edification, and to offer from the work of his hands to the Lord Himself through the needy. 3. He who does not work does not deserve his food (Mt 10:10; 2 Thess 3:10). 4. Work spurs us on to diligence.

10.31.3.en: v Whoever is able, let him work and give to the needy; and whoever is unwilling to work is condemned, and is counted unworthy even to eat (Mt 10:10; Acts 20:35) [36].

10.31.4.en: v We must, when possible, work, so that we may share our resources with those who lack them [37].

10.31.5.en: v The prohibition of excessive concern for the needs of our body does not abolish concern and work altogether.

10.31.6.en: For it remains for us to work for ourselves, not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life (Jn 6:27), not for our bodily needs only, but also to relieve our neighbor (Eph 4:28). And the Lord will say to us on the day of judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:35). What we do for those who have consecrated themselves to Him is counted as if we were working with them, and the heavenly Kingdom is given to us for it. On the contrary, those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and serve their neighbor will be punished (Acts 20:4, 35), and He will send them to eternal torment (Mt 25:41–46) [38].

10.32.0.en: 31 My son, glorify your soul with meekness, and give it the honor it deserves. 32 He who sins against himself, who will justify him? And who will honor him who dishonors his own life? 33 The poor man is honored for his work, and the rich man is honored for his riches. 34 He who is honored in poverty, how much more in riches? And he who is dishonored in riches, how much more in poverty?

10.32.1.en: My son, glorify your soul with humility, and give it honor according to its worth [28].

10.32.2.en: In the garden of Gethsemane the Lord bowed down to receive the cup of suffering from the hand of the Father, assuring us that in Him we seek the glory that God prepares for us: "Glorify thou me..." (Jn 17:5). And as Ben Sira warns us against self-importance, he also warns us against faintheartedness, which drives us into a state of frustration.

10.32.3.en: v When you insult, it is you who are insulted. Most people know this in part, when they say to one another: "Come, let us withdraw; do not dishonor yourself." Why? Because the difference between you and him is great. For when you insult him greatly, he counts this as credit to himself. Let us put this down in all cases, and rise above insults. I will tell you how.

10.32.4.en: Is it fitting for us to enter into a quarrel with one who wears purple? Let us reckon that when we insult him we are only insulting ourselves, since we are qualifying ourselves to be in shame. Tell me, what do you mean by this? When you are a citizen of heaven and have the heavenly philosophy, do you dishonor yourself with that man who minds earthly things? (Phil 3:19). For even though he possesses countless riches, and even though he has authority, yet he does not know the good that is in these things. Do not insult yourself by your insult of him... Honor yourself, not him. Is there not such a saying: that he who is honored honors himself? Because of what is good, he who honors honors not the other but himself. Hear what the wise man says: "Glorify your soul with honor from that source" (see Sir 10:28) [39].

10.32.5.en: St. John Chrysostom Who will justify a man who sins against himself, his soul?

10.32.6.en: And who will honor a man who dishonors his life? [29]

10.32.7.en: Ben Sira warns us against a man's belittling of him to whom God has given abilities, gifts and potentials.

10.32.8.en: The poor man is honored for his knowledge, and the rich man is honored for his riches [30].

10.32.9.en: There is that for which the poor man is honored, namely knowledge, wisdom and piety.

10.32.10.en: If a man is honored while in poverty, how much more while in wealth?

10.32.11.en: And if a man is dishonored while in wealth, how much more while in poverty? [31]

10.32.12.en: A wonderful, musical poetry that needs no interpretation. For if he who receives honor while poor because of his wisdom, what if he were to become rich? And if he who is dishonored because of his folly and his evil while rich, what if he were also to become poor?!

10.33.s.en: Grant me the spirit of wise leadership!

10.33.0.en: v O my God, You are the King of kings, You came down to raise up even from among children leaders full of love and wisdom.

10.33.1.en: You created human beings not that some of them should be slaves, but that all should bear the icon of wise leadership!

10.33.2.en: Everyone who cleaves to You becomes a king, with authority over his depths.

10.33.3.en: And by love even little children become mature heroes.

10.33.4.en: Teach me, train me, O You who are all meekness and humility.

10.33.5.en: Pour out Your grace within me, that I may enjoy the spirit of attractive leadership!

10.33.6.en: Sanctify me, that my inner Jerusalem may be sanctified by You. Let Your Kingdom be established within me!

10.33.7.en: v You raised the boy David to be king, and many long to be counted sons of David the successful leader.

10.33.8.en: And King Saul exalted himself, and his depths were filled with a spirit of vengeance against the one who rescued him again and again!

10.33.9.en: He corrupted his household, and he and his sons died in shame, and the throne was withdrawn from under him.

10.33.10.en: v Keep me lest I be lax with Belshazzar king of Babylon (Dan 5), who collapsed, he and his kingdom, in marvelous shame!

10.33.11.en: Truly You permitted him to be set up as a corrupt king over a corrupt people, so that the nations might be disciplined throughout the ages.

10.33.12.en: You are wise, O Lord, You who govern history, You send to every nation a leader for its edification or for its discipline!

10.33.13.en: v Grant me the spirit of earnestness without laxity, that Your hand may be stretched out and carry me successfully on the way of truth.

10.33.14.en: David listened to Your voice through the wise Abigail.

10.33.15.en: David blessed her, for she kept him from avenging himself on her husband Nabal the fool.

10.33.16.en: Grant me, O Lord, to listen with David to Your law, whoever the speaker of it may be!

10.33.17.en: Let not wrath creep into my heart toward him who causes me harm. And do not allow my mouth to utter a word of insult.

10.33.18.en: Lead my heart and my mouth Yourself, and set a strict guard over them. Sanctify them, that I may bear witness to You, O Holy One!

10.33.19.en: v Remove from me the spirit of anger, and grant me of Your meekness! Break down in me all pride, that I may enjoy Your humility!

10.33.20.en: Let Your Kingdom dwell within me, and be revealed in my depths.

10.33.21.en: I long to see every child a king and a leader, trampling under his feet the enemy of good and all his powers, and no thief able to steal his glory!

10.33.22.en: v Help me not to lose Your gift to me, for You want me to be a loving, humble and chaste leader.

10.33.23.en: Take away from me hatred and pride and the love of money.

10.33.24.en: You created me from dust and ashes, and granted me that my heart should be lifted up to Your heavens! Let me cleave to You, and not turn back from You!

10.33.25.en: Draw my depths up to Your heavens, that I may not wallow in the mire of this world.

10.33.26.en: Do not take from me Your grace that upheld the heavenly orders.

10.33.27.en: Lest sin drag me down to the abyss, and I join the powers of darkness.

10.33.28.en: v Rescue me from the tyrant of pride, who is the beginning of every sin, and grant me to fulfill Your holy will and not my evil will.

10.33.29.en: Grant me a zealous and humble heart, that I may not fall under punishment with the arrogant devil.

10.33.30.en: v Grant me what You gave to the Gentile king of Nineveh.

10.33.31.en: In humility he did not despise Your prophet Jonah, simple in his appearance.

10.33.32.en: He left the throne of the kingdom and put on sackcloth in sincere repentance.

10.33.33.en: He realized that there is no salvation except through the people's fellowship with their leaders, so that even the children took part in crying out to You.

10.33.34.en: The pagan king believed that the cry of the simple children and infants is stronger than every weapon!

10.33.35.en: Grant me, by the spirit of humility, to seek Your great mercies together with all the people.

10.33.36.en: v Grant me not to know old age, but to work for You and by Your grace until the last breath.

10.33.37.en: Let me work even on my deathbed!

11.0.s.en: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

11.0.0.en: 1 The wisdom of the lowly lifts up his head, and seats him among the assembly of the great. 2 Do not praise a man for his beauty, nor despise a man for his appearance. 3 The bee is small among the birds, and its harvest is the chief of all sweetness. 4 Do not boast of the wretchedness of your clothes, nor exalt yourself in the day of honor; for the works of the Lord are wonderful, and His deeds are hidden from men. 5 Many of those in authority have sat on the dust, and the obscure has worn the crown. 6 Many of the mighty have suffered the utmost disgrace, and the honored have been delivered into the hands of others.

11.0.1.en: The wisdom of the humble man lifts up his head, and his seat will be among the great [1].

11.0.2.en: The most dangerous thing in social relationships in general is appraising persons by outward appearance without careful study of the reality of their characters. For a man is often deceived by physical beauty, a gentle voice, elegance of dress, and a person's material level or social position. It would be fitting for a person to look at his brother or friend with regard to his true wisdom.

11.0.3.en: The wisdom of the humble person is like a passport by which he passes through life, whether in poverty or wealth, in distress or relief, in sickness or health. He sets out, and true, humble wisdom seats him among the great. But the fool supposes, by his possessions and wealth and gifts and studies and strength and outward appearance, that he is able to storm the councils of the great ones of the world, and even to sit at their head, not knowing that what he does reveals his weaknesses and folly and pride, so that he goes down in the eyes of God and in the eyes of many to sit as on a dunghill. This is what led the Apostle Paul to advise us that a man ought not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly (Rom 12:3).

11.0.4.en: He who acquires wisdom goes forth in a spirit of humility to the last rows with the Lord of glory Jesus, who became a servant and was crucified between two wicked thieves, and so the Lord of glory carries him, and he enters with his heart and mind into the heavenly sanctuaries. But he who walks in pride, in folly, collapses with the devil unless he returns to himself by repentance.

11.0.5.en: When God delivered Hannah from the humiliation she suffered from her rival Peninnah, she praised Him, saying: "The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength... The LORD killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and he hath set the world upon them (1 Sam 2:4-8).

11.0.6.en: v Be vigilant and be steadfast in the Lord. If you keep these sayings you will be good in everything. For it is written: glory goes before the humble (Prov 23:29); and also: "The wisdom of the humble lifts up his head" (Sir 1:11); and also: "But to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 2:66).

11.0.7.en: v It is also written: "The crushed bones rejoice" (Ps 8:50) (LXX); and also: "The prayer of the humble man is quickly accepted" (see Sir 32:17). And it is also written: "Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins" (Ps 18:25). See then the measure (of the greatness) of humility. If you have acquired humility you have acquired everything.

11.1.0.en: St. Abba Paula of Tamouh On humility Do not praise a man for the beauty of his appearance, and do not shun a man for his looks [2].

11.1.1.en: True glory does not rest on outward appearance, which often deceives a man, whether in choosing a life partner or the staff to work with him, even though history reveals the deception of appearances. We do not learn from the mistakes of former generations.

11.1.2.en: The prophet Samuel was amazed at the beauty of Saul the son of Kish and his stature, for it is said: "And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people" (1 Sam 9:2). "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the eyes, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7)

11.1.3.en: v Why are you troubled at a lack of beauty, since this is not shameful? Hear the saying of the wise man: "Do not praise a man for his beauty, nor shun a man for his appearance" (see Sir 10:2). Rather let God be the one who admires (you), the greatest Artist, not man, who has no merit in the make-up in which he was created. Tell me, what are the benefits of beauty? None. It exposes its possessor to great and dangerous trials, regrettable incidents and suspicions. For he who lacks beauty is spared suspicion, while he who possesses it must guard himself in an extremely unnatural way, and gives a poor account. And worse than this is the suspicion of the husband, who has less enjoyment by holding on to her beauty, and also suffers the troubles of jealousy over her. Her beauty becomes dim in his eyes because of her modesty, and she suffers in her character from the weak and from those given to amusement and licentiousness, so that her spirit collapses and she is filled with vanity [2].

11.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The bee is small among the flying creatures, but its fruit is the first among sweet things [3].

11.2.1.en: St. Augustine sees that the bee resembles some flying insects in outward appearance [3]. But how great is the difference between the bee that provides us with honey and some insects that cause us diseases.

11.2.2.en: The bee also, in its appearance, is a dangerous insect that stings a man and causes him pain, while it provides humanity with useful food, which is counted a considerable wealth for the nations. And St. John Chrysostom sees that the talk here is for the husband who sees that his wife lacks beauty, looking to another, for he says:

11.2.3.en: v "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:26-27). By the washing, or in the font, He washed her from defilement. And by the word, what word? "In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19). Not only did He adorn her, but He made her "glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing." Let us then seek this beauty for ourselves, and we can bring it about.

11.2.4.en: Do not ask of your wife's hand things which you cannot acquire. Do you not see that the Church has everything in the hand of her Lord? By Him she became glorious, and by Him she became pure without blame?

11.3.0.en: Do not turn your back on your wife because of a deformity in her. Hear what the Scripture says: "The bee is little among such as fly, but her fruit is the chief of sweet things" (see Sir 11:3). She is the work of God. Do not accuse her, but accuse her Creator, for what can a woman do? Praise her not for her beauty, for praise rests on the beauty that belongs to the soul... Let her seek the beauty of the soul. Imitate the Bridegroom of the Church. Outward beauty is full of deception and great dissolution, it drives people to envy, and it drives you to expect hideous things [4].

11.4.0.en: v Solomon also does something similar, for he returns to one who lives as in an idle life and confronts him with the ant (Prov 6:6-8), and here he confronts him with the bee [5].

11.5.0.en: v If you see a huge man with good qualities, and tall, surpassing others in the length of his limbs, do not marvel at him until you are sure of the state of his soul. It is fitting for us to proclaim a man and call him blessed not for the beauty of his appearance, but for the beauty that relates to the soul. David was small in his body, and short in stature, and though he was so short and small of body, and his arms bare (without weapons), he brought down upon a great army with a single blow that body which was like a tower, without hurling an arrow or drawing a sword from its sheath, but did all this with a little stone. For this reason we were advised thus: "Do not praise a man for his beauty... The bee is small among the flying creatures, but what she gathers is the chief of all sweetness" (see Sir 11:2-3) [6].

11.5.1.en: St. John Chrysostom Do not boast of your splendid clothes, and do not exalt yourself on the day when you are glorified, for the works of the Lord are wonderful, and His deeds are hidden from men [4].

11.5.2.en: Sometimes a man's character can be discovered from his dress, yet some exaggerate in wearing luxurious clothes to hide their meager characters. Some great philosophers, men of learning and those consecrated to service are not much occupied with their clothing. These are content with simplicity of appearance without vulgarity or noticeable neglect. He who realizes the value of the beauty of his soul, which the Holy Spirit of God adorns, feels an inner satisfaction, and does not wait for a word of praise for his outward appearance.

11.5.3.en: v Our teacher advises us plainly: "Do not boast of the clothes you wear, and do not exalt yourself on the day of your glory, for it does not last" [4]. And more plainly he speaks mockingly of those who wear soft clothing, saying in the Gospel: "Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts" (Lk 7:25). He means these earthly courts that crumble, where vanity and empty glory and flattery and error dwell. But those who serve the heavenly court of the King of all sanctify their bodies, which are the worn-out garments of their souls, and clothe them with incorruption [7].

11.6.0.en: v Let us pursue that (true) glory, and not that in which there is something grand. Let us leave the glory of the world as a trifle. "Do not boast of the clothes you wear" (see Sir 11:4). Truly, dancers and harlots and actresses wear brighter and far costlier clothes than you. Besides, this boasting is of the kind that the moth attacks, and it can rob you of your joy [8].

11.6.1.en: St. John Chrysostom Many of the tyrants sit on the dust, but he who was not in the reckoning wears the crown [5].

11.6.2.en: Many rulers are overtaken by the utmost disgrace, and the glorified are delivered into the hands of others [6].

11.6.3.en: "He leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools. He looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle. He leadeth priests away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty. He removeth away the speech of the trusted, and taketh away the understanding of the aged. He poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty" (Job 12:17-21).

11.7.s.en: 2. True wisdom and not being hasty

11.7.0.en: 7 Do not blame before you examine. Understand first, then rebuke. 8 Do not answer before you hear, and do not interrupt a man's speech before he has finished.

11.7.1.en: Do not condemn before you examine the case, but first understand, then judge [7].

11.8.0.en: Do not answer before you hear, and do not interrupt a speaker while he is speaking [8].

11.9.0.en: v Do not let the stirring up of quarrels, through our love of empty victory, creep in among us. Our aim is to exclude every dispute. Surely this is the meaning of the phrase: "Peace be unto you" (Jn 20:19, 21), "Do not answer before you hear" (11:8). The indistinct voice is the voice of a womanish man; at any rate the voice of the self-controlled man is moderate in its tone, so that it is neither too loud nor talkative, nor does he speak rapidly, nor is he long-winded in speech [9].

11.10.s.en: 3. True wisdom and work without planning

11.10.0.en: 9 Do not dispute about a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners. 10 My son, do not busy yourself with many works; for if you multiply them you will not be free from blame. If you pursue them you will not overtake them, and if you outrun them you will not escape. 11 There is a man who labors and toils and strives, and only becomes more in want!

11.10.1.en: Do not dispute about a matter that is not your concern, and do not sit with sinners when they judge a case [9].

11.10.2.en: By the spirit of discernment the man of God realizes the truth of his obligations, and so works wisely within the limits of his responsibilities, instead of wasting his time on what is not his concern. Here he calls us to avoid dealing with two groups that waste time: the group of those who love disputing about matters that are not our concern, such as analyzing political events and arguing about them, while he is unable even to express his opinion because he does not know the facts. And the second group is keeping up with unjust judges in a kind of hypocrisy and partiality.

11.11.0.en: My son, do not let your work include many things, for if you multiply them, you will not continue without punishment; even if you advance in them, you will not overtake them, and you will not escape by fleeing [10].

11.11.1.en: It is fitting for us not to be occupied with many works and achievements, but to keep to faithfulness until we hear the divine voice: "You have been faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things" (Mt 25:21).

11.12.0.en: There is a man who works and works and keeps on working, yet becomes poorer [11].

11.12.1.en: Many are occupied with the number of hours they spend at work, and not with working faithfully and wisely so that it may be fruitful. Let us remember our need to seek the blessing of the Lord; for in many works a man can accomplish in one hour a work that previously needed a whole day. It is said that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8). This is felt by the student when he is troubled and realizes that his achievement in study is weak, and when his soul is filled with peace and joy his achievement in study is very good. Also, at times a man works diligently and strongly, but with pride and arrogance, and so loses much, and even loses the salvation of his soul and his eternity.

11.13.s.en: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

11.13.0.en: 12 And there is a man who is slow, in need of help, lacking strength, in great poverty, 13 yet the eyes of the Lord looked upon him for good, and raised him up from his lowliness, and lifted up his head so that many marveled at him. 14 Good and evil, life and death, poverty and wealth are from the Lord. 15 Wisdom and knowledge and understanding of the Law are from the Lord. Love and the ways of good works are from Him. 16 Error and darkness were created with sinners, and those who delight in evil grow old in evil. 17 The gift of the Lord remains with the godly, and His good pleasure prospers forever.

11.13.1.en: And there is another who is lazy and needs help, strength is lacking in him and he grows poorer, yet the eyes of the Lord look upon him for his good, and He restores his good from his lowly state [12]. Many, even among the famous and the great and the heroes, when they compare the praise of people for them with the truth of their capabilities, fall into a state of frustration, and it turns into a psychological illness. Here He offers them the remedy, which is faith that God fixes His eyes on man because he is His beloved; by His grace He raises him up and grants him self-confidence.

11.14.0.en: He lifts up his head, and many are amazed at this [13].

11.14.1.en: The wise Solomon looks at history and sees horsemen famed for courage and for the ability to enter battles, who won victories, yet some of them fell suddenly in defeat. For this it was fitting for them to realize that victory is from the Lord. "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:31)

11.15.0.en: Good and evil, life and death, and poverty and wealth are from the Lord [14]... [10]

11.15.1.en: The Holy Bible affirms two truths that touch man's life: that God gave man freedom of will so that he might be responsible for his actions, and the second, that the mind is a surpassing gift so that it may manage man's life with understanding.

11.15.2.en: Concerning freedom of will, it is said:

11.15.3.en: v God, as good and loving (generous), gave man freedom with regard to good and evil, granting him a mind by which he is able to behold the world and all that is in it, and so to know God for whose sake He created everything. As for the evil man, he may desire this (the knowledge of God), but he does not understand, rather he perishes through his unbelief and his thinking that contradicts the truth. This is man's freedom with regard to good and evil [11].

11.15.4.en: St. Anthony the Great v (Adam was free to pluck or not to pluck the deadly fruit).

11.15.5.en: Try what I say by these things that are your own, so that the solution of your doubts may come from your own thinking.

11.15.6.en: You have authority to plant or not to plant a plant, and in your hands is the possibility of doing either of the two.

11.15.7.en: If you wish to plant a vine it becomes a vine, and if you do not wish, you will not plant it and it will not become so.

11.15.8.en: Thus the Just One gave freedom to Adam whom He formed; it was within his authority to keep himself from harms.

11.15.9.en: That command was appointed for that freedom, that it might be led by its own will to where it wishes.

11.15.10.en: He set a fence for it: that Law, lest the evil seed enter into it like a stranger who does not belong to it.

11.15.11.en: She opened the door and the crafty one entered and cast his seed, and the land of the soul, which had been a paradise, was corrupted.

11.15.12.en: Evil grew and became a tree full of death, and it returned and gave the fruits of death to the one who planted it.

11.15.13.en: As Moses guided the people while teaching them (saying): Look to your heart, let there be no abominable iniquity in it.

11.15.14.en: Thus the Father commanded Adam not to eat, that is, do not receive in yourself an evil seed [12].

11.15.15.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh As for the relation of the mind to the soul and the body, St. Anthony the Great speaks to us, saying:

11.15.16.en: v Life is a union between the mind (spirit), the soul and the body, and a bond among them, while death is the tearing apart of this unity, but there is no perishing of all these (elements), rather God preserves them even after the separation [13].

11.15.17.en: v The mind that pleases God flows before the soul and counsels it to despise the temporal, material, perishable things, and to love the eternal, incorruptible spiritual blessings, so that man, while still in the body, perceives the heavenly and divine things with his mind and contemplates them. By this the mind that loves God is profitable to the soul and its rescuer.

11.15.18.en: v The souls that are not bridled by the mind, and not governed by the intellect, which suppresses their passions of pleasures and pains, and manages them and directs them (rightly), these souls perish like the irrational animals. For their minds are drawn by the passions, as unruly horses drag their drivers.

11.15.19.en: v The soul is in the body, and the mind is in the soul, and the Word is in the mind, and by the Word we contemplate God and glorify Him, who gives immortality to the soul and grants it eternal, incorruptible happiness.

11.15.20.en: St. Anthony the Great v The adornment of the body is the mind, and the adornment of the mind is God [14].

11.15.21.en: St. Augustine The view of the wise man toward wealth: when the believer is in touch with the Lord's care, he is not disturbed by poverty, nor does he exalt himself because of wealth. All that occupies him is cleaving to the Lord.

11.16.0.en: v If you regard wealth and the fullness of its enjoyment as nothing but a deceptive show of pride for a short time, and you know that the virtuous life that pleases God is better than wealth, and you hold fast to this belief and keep it in your memory, then you will never sigh nor murmur nor rebuke anyone, but you will give thanks to God in every circumstance, even if you see people worse than you being praised for their eloquence or knowledge or wealth. The desire for wealth with greed and for pleasures, and the love of lust and vainglory, joined with ignorance of the truth, bring the worst sufferings of the soul [15].

11.16.1.en: St. Anthony the Great The gift of the Lord remains with the godly, and His good pleasure brings prosperity forever [15].

11.16.2.en: The wise man says: "Good and evil, life and death, and poverty and wealth are from the Lord" (see Sir 11:14). Some ask whether God is the source of evil as He is the source of good. Is God, the Giver of life, the fountain of life and the fountain of death? Is the Giver of gifts the source of poverty as of wealth?

11.17.0.en: v The cause of death is Satan, he who deceived man, but God brought upon him the punishment of death not as one who first issued (the command of death), but as a (natural) punishment for sin. You yourself answered the question perfectly when you said that man was left to himself, and so he became a torment to himself, through the judgment of God, and this was accomplished by his free will. There is no contradiction in the fact that man himself is the source of his punishment, and that God takes vengeance on sin [16].

11.17.1.en: St. Augustine v Open to us, O Lord, the treasury, at the prayers of our supplications.

11.17.2.en: Let our prayers serve as an ambassador for us, and reconcile us with Your divinity.

11.17.3.en: Hearken, O wise men, and give heed, all you who are learners.

11.18.0.en: Seek understanding and knowledge, seeing that you are learners and wise (in the Lord) [17].

11.18.1.en: St. Mar Ephraim the Syrian v When you see a corpse carried in the market, followed by orphaned children, and a widow beating her breast, and servants wailing, and friends depressed, consider the triviality of present things, and that they do not differ at all from a shadow or a dream. Does this not suit you? Think of those who were very rich and perished in the war. Look at the houses around you, which belonged to famous great men, and now have come down to the ground.

11.19.0.en: Consider how powerful they were, and now no memory at all has been left for them. And if you wish, you will find every day examples of these things: from the quarrels of rulers, and the confiscation of the property of the rich. Many tyrants have sat on the dust, and he who never thought of it has put on the crown" (see Sir 11:15). Are not our affairs like a wheel? [18]

11.20.0.en: 18 There is a rich man who has grown rich by his care and thrift, and this is the portion of his reward, 19 when he says: "I have found rest, and now I will eat of my goods," 20 and he does not know how much time will pass until he leaves it to others and dies. 21 Stand fast in your covenant, and be busy in it, and grow old in your work. 22 Do not marvel at the works of sinners. Trust in the Lord and abide in your labor. 23 For it is easy in the eyes of the Lord to make the poor man rich suddenly, in an instant. 24 The blessing of the Lord is in the reward of the godly, and in a moment He makes his blessing flourish. 25 Do not say: "What need have I, and what good shall come to me from now on?" 26 Do not say: "I have enough, so why should I toil from now on?"

11.20.1.en: The Lord Christ explained this saying to us by the parable of the rich man who thought that his possessions would give his soul satisfaction for many years, and did not know that his soul would be required of him that very night (Lk 12:16-21).

11.20.2.en: There is a man who grows rich by his care and thrift, and this is the portion of his reward: [16]

11.20.3.en: when he says: "I have found rest, and now I will share my goods," and he does not know how much time will pass until he dies and leaves that to others [17].

11.20.4.en: It is among the most grievous things that a man should spend all his life preparing what he will possess for the future in this world, not knowing what will befall. His position is very pitiable, since he puts his hope in the wrong place. For wealth can keep a man from many troubles, but it cannot drive death away from its owner. Death robs a man of what he consecrated his life to acquiring. This is what the parable of the rich man affirmed, who built many of his storehouses to eat and drink and be merry, and he heard the voice of the Lord: "Fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" (Lk 12:16-20). This parable presents two warnings: preparation for passing from this world; and avoidance of covetousness.

11.20.5.en: The catastrophe is not in the person's death but in his lack of preparation for passing from the world, and the loss of his whole life in gathering what he will leave behind involuntarily; therefore the Lord called him "fool" (Lk 12:20).

11.20.6.en: Stand fast in your covenant, and care for it, and reach old age in your work [18].

11.20.7.en: v Let no one think that the Apostle differs from these words of ours by saying: that they work quietly, and eat their own bread (2 Thess 3:11-12). This commandment is directed to the stubborn and the slack, and it means that it is better for every man to serve at least himself, and not be a burden on others and live idle... Again, his saying: "We wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:8), carries the same meaning. In the name of brotherly love the Apostle bore the burden of work, besides his obligation toward those who were committed to him, with the aim of eliminating disorder. He who strives passionately for perfection is bound to work night and day, "that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). The man who relies on himself, or even on another person who is bound to supply him with his needs, and thinks that his own activity and the activity of him who is gathered with him is enough to help him in his livelihood, falls into danger, for he puts his hope in a man, and so falls under the curse that says: "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD" (Jer 17:3).

11.21.0.en: Now by the saying: "trusteth in man," the Holy Bible forbids a man to put his hope in another. And by saying "maketh flesh his arm" it forbids him to rely on himself. In both cases there is a turning away from the Lord (that is, his heart departs from the Lord). Then it joins the two together by saying: "For he shall be like the tamaric in the desert (wilderness), and shall not see when good cometh" (Jer 17:6). The Holy Bible declares that any man who makes his reliance on himself or on anyone else turns himself away from the Lord [19].

11.21.1.en: v The prohibition of excessive concern for the needs of our body does not abolish concern and work altogether.

11.21.2.en: For it remains for us to work for ourselves, not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life (Jn 6:27), not for our bodily needs only, but also to relieve our neighbor (Eph 4:28). And the Lord will say to us on the day of judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:35). What we do for those who have consecrated themselves to Him is counted as if we were working with them, and the heavenly Kingdom is given to us for it.

11.22.0.en: And on the contrary, those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and serve their neighbor will be punished (Acts 20:4, 35), and He will send them to eternal torment (Mt 25:41–46) [20].

11.22.1.en: St. Basil the Great Do not marvel at the works of the sinner, but trust in the Lord and persevere in your work, for it is easy in the eyes of the Lord to make the poor man rich suddenly in an instant (without expectation) [19].

11.22.2.en: The blessing of the Lord is in the reward of the godly man, and in a moment God makes His blessing flourish [20].

11.22.3.en: Do not say: "What need have I?

11.23.0.en: And what good things shall I receive in the future?" [21]

11.23.1.en: Do not say: I am independent [21]. From now on what evil will befall me?" [22].

11.23.2.en: Man by nature, from childhood, tends to be self-sufficient, not depending on others. This inclination has its blessings if it is used with moderation and wisdom, and through it he feels a kind of independence. But if he isolates himself from God and does not trust in Him, this drives him to a kind of dictatorship and arrogance.

11.23.3.en: God upholds man that he may enjoy a sound personality, one of whose requirements is self-confidence, through the work of His divine grace, but not in conceit of himself and arrogance toward his Creator who cares for him.

11.24.s.en: 6. True wisdom and awaiting the end

11.24.0.en: 27 Afflictions are forgotten in the day of good things, and good things are not remembered in the day of afflictions. 28 For it is easy for the Lord to repay a man according to his ways on the day of death. 29 An hour of evil makes one forget pleasures, and at a man's death his works are revealed. 30 Call no one blessed before his death. A man is known by his sons.

11.24.1.en: In the day of good things, afflictions are forgotten, and in the day of afflictions good things are not remembered [23].

11.24.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job, in the midst of his afflictions, remembers the works he had done before, so that his soul might not be drawn to despair, but might take refuge in secure hope.

11.24.3.en: v (In a letter in which he speaks of the history of the sin of Fabiola and then of her repentance)

11.24.4.en: As I find my soul dashing against the weaknesses of Fabiola's sin, I have spoken much of it and of her repentance, that I may open a broad and calm way, unhindered, in order to describe her praise. She returned to communion before the eyes of the whole Church. What did she do? In the days of good things she forgot the afflictions (see Sir 11:23). And when her ship was wrecked she did not wish to face the dangers of the sea again. Therefore instead of returning to board the ship of her former life, she sold everything she could lay her hand on of her possessions (for they were great, befitting her rank), and turned it into cash and offered it for the benefit of the poor. If someone set up a hospital that gathered the sufferers in the streets, she would nurse them, and all the victims of diseases and want [22].

11.24.5.en: St. Jerome For it is easy for the Lord to reward a man on the day of his death according to his ways [24].

11.24.6.en: The hour of harsh treatment makes a man forget luxury, and at the end of a man's life his works are revealed [25].

11.24.7.en: It is hard to judge a person while he is still breathing, and even after his death the Church does not hasten to consider a person a saint.

11.24.8.en: v Nothing is against philosophy (wisdom) like a life of pleasure, and on the other hand, nothing is so profitable to philosophy as pain. Consider what the state of the covetous man will be. For it is said: "An hour of evil makes a man forget pleasures" (see Sir 11:25) [23].

11.24.9.en: St. John Chrysostom Do not consider anyone happy before his death, and a man will be known in his children [26].

11.24.10.en: The praise of the departed is better than the praise of the living: the wise, godly man, who fears the Lord, is praised at the close of his life, for a man's praise at the end of his life is better than his praise during his life.

11.24.11.en: v It is written that wisdom is known at death, meaning that the life of the wise man is praised at the end of his life. Therefore we read elsewhere: "Do not praise a man during his life, and do not call a man blessed before his death" (see Sir 11:26-28). Suppose a man says: I will praise a man after his death, because praising a living man can be an occasion for vainglory, because of the commendation of him or for flattery by him who offers the praise.
